steps.title: Rhône and beyond
steps.body: Viognier's home is the northern Rhône: Condrieu and Château-Grillet. It's grown in the Languedoc for IGP Pays d'Oc wines, and in California, Virginia, Australia's Eden Valley and Yalumba, and South Africa. Yalumba, in Australia, pioneered it there from 1980.

steps.title: Ripeness matters
steps.body: Viognier needs warmth to develop its perfume, but too much heat makes it flabby and alcoholic. It must be picked at full ripeness, when aromas peak; picked early, it tastes neutral; picked late, it loses acidity and gains bitterness. Like Gewürztraminer, the picking window is narrow.

steps.prompt: What happens if Viognier is picked too early?
steps.explanation: Its aromas develop late in ripening.

steps.title: With Syrah
steps.body: In Côte-Rôtie, up to 20% Viognier can be co-fermented with Syrah, though most use 2 to 5%. Co-fermentation stabilises colour, through a process called co-pigmentation, and adds floral lift. Australian producers adopted the idea for Shiraz Viognier.

steps.prompt: What does Viognier add when co-fermented with Syrah?
steps.explanation: Viognier is a white grape; it doesn't add tannin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viognier's home is Condrieu in the northern Rhône
It needs warmth and precise picking
In Côte-Rôtie it's co-fermented with Syrah
